## Objectives

- See what a principal component *is*: a direction, not a variable
- Read loadings, scores, and the scree plot — and stop at the right number
- Find the **latent drivers** behind twenty questionnaire items
- Meet the idea that comes back in week 5: compression as a model

## Why a manager cares

::: {.subtitle-frame}
Twenty questions, three answers
:::

| | Too many columns | The question | A few components |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Retailer** | 24 items in a satisfaction survey | what drives satisfaction? | two or three drivers |
| **Regional health service** | 30 quality indicators per hospital | which hospitals do well, and at what? | outcomes, efficiency |

: {tbl-colwidths="[22,30,26,22]"}

- A patient-experience survey asks about courtesy, clarity and waiting a dozen ways: it measures far fewer things than it has questions

In each case the data are **wide** and **redundant**. PCA finds the few directions along which they actually vary, and throws away the rest.

## [Section 1]{.section-kicker} The idea {.section-slide background-color="#002f57"}

## A component is a direction

::: {.subtitle-frame}
Stated without matrices first
:::

Picture the data as a cloud of $n$ points in $p$ dimensions.

- The **first principal component** is the line through the cloud along which the points are *most spread out*
- The **second** is the line at right angles to the first with the most remaining spread
- And so on, $p$ times — but the spread runs out fast

A point's **score** is its coordinate on that line; a variable's **loading**, how much it shapes the line.

::: {.callout-note}
Nothing is dropped yet: PCA is a *rotation*. Compression comes when you keep the first few components, and you decide how many.
:::

## The direction, found by looking for it

{{< video media/Rotation.mp4 width="880" height="495" >}}

Sixty wards, scored by patients on courtesy and clarity. The line turns and the variance of the projection is traced: its peak, at 32°, is PC1, with 89% of the spread.

## The same thing, in one line

For centred data $X$ ($n \times p$), the first component is the unit vector $\phi_1$ that maximises the variance of the projection:

$$
\phi_1 = \arg\max_{\lVert \phi \rVert = 1} \; \operatorname{Var}(X \phi)
$$

- The solution is the leading **eigenvector of the covariance matrix** $X^\top X / n$
- Its eigenvalue $\lambda_1$ is the variance it captures. $\lambda_1 / \sum_j \lambda_j$ is the *proportion of variance explained*
- Components 2, 3, … are the next eigenvectors, orthogonal to the previous ones

Everything you will read off a PCA is one of: a loading vector $\phi_k$, a score $X\phi_k$, or a variance share $\lambda_k / \sum \lambda$.

## By hand: two variables, perfectly correlated

Height and arm span of four patients, in tens of cm from the mean: $(-1.5,-1.5), (-0.5,-0.5), (0.5,0.5), (1.5,1.5)$. Each column has variance $1.25$: $2.5$ in total.

- The cloud is a line at 45°. The first component is that line: $\phi_1 = (0.707, 0.707)$
- Scores along it: $-2.12, -0.71, 0.71, 2.12$. Variance $= 2.5$: all of it
- The second component is perpendicular: $\phi_2 = (0.707, -0.707)$. Every score is $0$. Variance $= 0$.

**Two variables, one component, 100% of the variance.** Two columns, one piece of information: which is why arm span can stand in for height when a patient cannot stand.

[Variances divide by $n$, as in $X^\top X / n$. `prcomp` divides by $n - 1$ and prints $3.33$ and $0$: same shares.]{.muted}

## By hand, watched

{{< video media/PCAByHand.mp4 width="880" height="495" >}}

The four patients, every score written out: variance $1.25 + 1.25$ goes in, $2.5 + 0$ comes out. When two columns say the same thing, PCA says so with a number.

## Scale, again

PCA is a variance-hunter. A variable measured in thousands *is* the first component, whatever it means.

- **Standardise** — `scale. = TRUE` — unless every column is already in the same unit and you *want* the large-variance ones to dominate
- On a survey where every item is 1–5, you may leave it; on customer behaviour, you may not

::: {.callout-important title="Attention"}
Same trap as clustering, same fix, same reason. Distance and variance are both blind to units.
:::

## [Drill 1]{.drill-kicker} One score per hospital

::: {.subtitle-frame}
In pairs · 10 minutes · 120 invented hospitals · PC1 loadings, without and with `scale. = TRUE`
:::

| Indicator | PC1 raw · 99.99% | PC1 scaled · 47.5% |
|---|---|---|
| Cost per case (€) | −1.00 | −0.23 |
| Length of stay (days) | 0.00 | 0.03 |
| 30-day mortality (%) | 0.00 | 0.56 |
| 30-day readmissions (%) | 0.00 | 0.58 |
| Patient experience (0–100) | 0.00 | −0.55 |

: {tbl-colwidths="[44,28,28]"}

1. Raw, PC1 explains 99.99% of the variance. What is it, and why?
2. Scaled, which indicators carry PC1? What does a **high** score say about a hospital?
3. The region publishes one PC1 score per hospital. Which version? Defend it in **one sentence**.

## [Drill 1 · answer]{.drill-kicker} Euros are not more important, only bigger

- **Raw**: PC1 *is* the cost per case (−1.00, every other loading 0.00). Its variance is 422 278 euro², the next is patient experience at 38: the 99.99% measures a unit, not the hospitals
- **Scaled**: mortality (0.56), readmissions (0.58) and patient experience (−0.55) carry it. A high score is a hospital with **worse outcomes**: R chose the sign, so read it before ranking anyone
- Cost and length of stay move to PC2 (0.67, 0.72): efficiency is a second, separate story

::: {.callout-tip title="A sentence that defends it"}
"The scaled one: unscaled, the 'performance score' is the cost per case under another name, because euros are bigger numbers than percentages; scaled, it measures outcomes, which is what we publish."
:::

## [Section 2]{.section-kicker} How many, and what do they mean {.section-slide background-color="#002f57"}

## How many components to keep

- **Scree plot**: variance explained per component. Keep the ones before the curve flattens — the *elbow*, again
- **Cumulative share**: keep enough to reach 70–80% — a convention, not a law
- **Kaiser**: keep components with eigenvalue $> 1$ on standardised data, i.e. that explain more than one original variable's worth

They disagree often. When they do, prefer the smaller number you can **interpret**. A component nobody can name is not a driver; it is noise with a label.

## Three rules, three answers

{{< video media/ScreeChoice.mp4 width="880" height="495" >}}

168 patients with lung cancer (`survival::lung`, six measures, standardised): the elbow keeps one component, Kaiser two, 80% four. The choice is yours to defend.

## Naming a component

Read its loadings: large positive and large negative ones tell you what the direction *contrasts*. Here, a private clinic's patient survey (invented, 400 patients).

| Item | PC1 | PC2 |
|---|---|---|
| Staff courtesy | **0.58** | −0.05 |
| Waiting time | **0.56** | −0.04 |
| Clarity of explanations | **0.58** | −0.06 |
| Price fairness | 0.07 | **0.70** |
| Value for money | 0.06 | **0.70** |

PC1: *service experience*. PC2: *price perception*. Two drivers, from five items — and now a regression of satisfaction on **two** scores instead of five collinear columns.

## In R

```{.r code-line-numbers="1-2|4|6-7|9-10|12"}
library(tidyverse); library(factoextra)
X <- USArrests                                  # 50 states, 4 crime rates + urban pop

pca <- prcomp(X, scale. = TRUE)

summary(pca)                                    # variance explained, cumulative
fviz_eig(pca)                                   # scree

pca$rotation                                    # loadings: variable × component
head(pca$x)                                     # scores: state × component

fviz_pca_biplot(pca, repel = TRUE)              # both at once — the plot to show
```

::: {.callout-note}
On `USArrests`, PC1 is the three crime rates, *overall crime*; PC2 is *urbanisation*. Two components, 87% of the variance, both named.
:::

## The biplot, read properly

- **Points** are observations, placed by their scores on PC1 and PC2
- **Arrows** are variables, drawn from their loadings
- A long arrow: the variable is well represented in these two components
- Two arrows at a small angle: the variables are correlated. At 90°: not. Opposite: negatively.
- A point far out along an arrow scores high on that variable

It is the single most information-dense plot in this course. Spend the lab learning to read one.

## [Drill 2]{.drill-kicker} How fit is the patient?

::: {.subtitle-frame}
In pairs · 10 minutes · the clip's 168 patients, `survival::lung` · loadings from `prcomp(scale. = TRUE)`
:::

| | Age | ECOG, doctor | Karnofsky, doctor | Karnofsky, patient | Calories at meals | Weight lost |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **PC1** · $\lambda = 2.56$ | −0.33 | −0.55 | 0.55 | 0.47 | 0.18 | −0.19 |
| **PC2** · $\lambda = 1.08$ | −0.36 | 0.23 | −0.29 | −0.05 | 0.81 | −0.26 |

: {tbl-colwidths="[22,10,13,14,14,14,13]"}

[ECOG: 0 no symptoms … 4 bedbound. Karnofsky: 100 no complaints, lower is worse.]{.muted}

1. Which measures carry PC1, with which sign? What does a **high** PC1 score say about a patient?
2. Kaiser keeps PC2. What is it, read from its loadings?
3. One component or two? The **one sentence** for the oncology unit's manager.

## [Drill 2 · answer]{.drill-kicker} One component, and it has a name

- **PC1** (43% of the variance): Karnofsky by the doctor (0.55) and by the patient (0.47), ECOG against them (−0.55). A high score is a **fitter patient**: *functional status*
- **PC2** (18%): calories at meals (0.81) and little else. One measure is not a driver; Kaiser keeps it only because 1.08 clears 1 by 0.08
- **Keep one**: the elbow's answer, and the only component with a name

::: {.callout-tip title="A sentence that defends it"}
"One: it is where the scree flattens, and it is the only component we can name, how fit the patient is, read from the doctor's scores and the patient's own; the second is the calories column, so if it matters we use the column."
:::

## [Section 3]{.section-kicker} Compression as a model {.section-slide background-color="#002f57"}

## PCA reconstructs

Keep $q < p$ components. From the scores you can *rebuild* an approximation of every row:

$$
\hat X \;=\; (X \Phi_q)\, \Phi_q^\top
$$

- $q = p$: perfect reconstruction. $q = 1$: each row is replaced by its projection on one line
- The reconstruction error $\lVert X - \hat X \rVert^2$ is exactly the variance you threw away

::: {.callout-note}
Hold this thought for week 5. A neural network that learns to compress its input to $q$ numbers and rebuild it is called an **autoencoder** — and with linear activations, it *is* PCA. Nonlinear activations make it a PCA that can bend.
:::

## A component is what your variables have in common. Naming it is your job, not the algorithm's.  {.statement}
